method_card.title: Factorising quadratics (a ≠ 1)
steps: Multiply \(a \times c\) to get a target product.
Find two numbers that multiply to \(ac\) and add to \(b\).
Split the middle term \(bx\) into those two terms.
Factorise in pairs and take out the common bracket.
method_card.content:
When \(a \neq 1\) you cannot just find two numbers that multiply to \(c\); you must aim for the product \(ac\). This is the ac method, or splitting the middle term.

Find two numbers that multiply to \(ac\) and add to \(b\), rewrite the middle term as those two terms, then factorise in pairs and pull out the shared bracket. Always expand your answer to check it gives the original quadratic.
method_card.example:
Factorise \(3x^2 + 10x + 3\)

\(ac = 9\); two numbers multiply to 9 and add to 10: 1 and 9. Split: \(3x^2 + x + 9x + 3 = x(3x+1) + 3(3x+1)\). Answer: \((x+3)(3x+1)\).

misconceptions.message: This is \(a \neq 1\), so the simple method fails; multiply \(a \times c\) first, then find the factor pair.
Check the signs inside the brackets; flipping both signs changes the sign of the middle term.

problem_bank.bronze_description: Factorise quadratics with small positive coefficients.
problem_bank.silver_description: Include negative terms and slightly larger coefficients.
problem_bank.gold_description: Larger leading numbers and products, with mixed signs.

bronze.title: Bronze: factorising with small positive numbers
steps: Multiply a by c (the number in front of \(x^2\) times the constant). This is your target product.
Find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to the middle number b. With all-positive terms both numbers are positive.
Split the middle term into those two pieces, then factorise in pairs to reveal the shared bracket.

steps.label: Factor pair
steps.content: Two numbers multiply to 12 and add to 7: \(3\) and \(4\).

silver.title: Silver: factorising with negative terms
steps: Multiply a by c as before, but watch the sign: a negative constant makes the product negative.
Find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to b. A negative product means one number is positive and one is negative.
Split the middle term and factorise in pairs, keeping every sign as you go.

gold.title: Gold: large products and mixed signs
steps: Multiply a by c. With larger leading numbers the product can be big, so list the factor pairs carefully.
Pick the pair that multiplies to \(ac\) and adds to b, choosing signs so the product and the sum both come out right.
Split, group in pairs, pull out the common bracket, then expand to check.

steps.say: A puzzle first, no algebra needed. A rectangular garden has an area of 12 m², and its two side lengths are whole numbers that add up to 7 m.

steps.pre: The shorter side, in metres, is
steps.hint: Which two whole numbers multiply to 12 (the area) and add to 7? Try 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4.

steps.pre: and the longer side, in metres, is
steps.hint: The two sides multiply to the area, 12, so the partner of 3 is 12 ÷ 3.

steps.say: You just found two numbers from a target product (12) and a target sum (7). That hunt is the whole engine of factorising \(ax^2+bx+c\): the product you aim for is \(a \times c\), and the sum you aim for is the middle number \(b\). The rest is just splitting and bracketing.
When the number in front of \(x^2\) is not 1, use the ac method. First multiply that front number, \(a\), by the constant, \(c\).
Now find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to the middle number, 7.

steps.hint: Add 3 and 4; it should equal the middle number.
steps.done: They hit 12 and 7, so 3 and 4 are the numbers.

steps.say: Split the middle term: \(2x^2 + 3x + 4x + 6\). Group in pairs: \(x(2x+3) + 2(2x+3)\), giving \((x+2)(2x+3)\).

steps.pre: Check the constant: multiply the two second numbers, 2 × 3 =
steps.hint: Multiply the 2 and the 3 inside the brackets.
steps.done: It matches the +6 in the question, so \((x+2)(2x+3)\) is right.

steps.say: Same method, but now a term is negative. Multiply \(a\) by \(c\), keeping the sign.

steps.hint: A positive times a negative is negative.

steps.say: Find two numbers that multiply to \(-12\) and add to the middle number, 1. A negative product means one number is positive and one is negative.

steps.done: They hit −12 and 1, so 4 and −3 are the numbers.

steps.pre: Check the constant: multiply the two second numbers, (−3) × 2 =
steps.done: It matches the −6 in the question, so \((2x-3)(x+2)\) is right.

steps.say: A bigger leading number, but the method does not change. Multiply \(a\) by \(c\).
Find two numbers that multiply to \(-18\) and add to the middle number, 7. One is positive, one is negative.

steps.done: They hit −18 and 7, so 9 and −2 are the numbers.

steps.done: It matches the −3 in the question, so \((3x-1)(2x+3)\) is right.
